This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Ohio's Republican candidate for Governor Vivek Ramaswamy is behind an attack ad featuring
the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.
This tight race has become a deeply personal contest to govern the Buckeye State.
George Shilcock with Member Station WOSU in Columbus has the latest.
In the ad, Acton's mother Donna Arthur claims Acton lied about growing up homeless and living
in a tent.
Court records prove Acton wasn't lying.
Acton says she hasn't spoken to her mother in 50 years.
Arthur's custody was revoked after Acton's now deceased stepfather was accused of raping
her.
Arthur sided with her husband over her daughter in the case.
It's awful to see her this way and it's even more incredible to see that my opponent has
taken advantage of someone who is clearly not well.
Ramaswamy tells the Associated Press and other reporters his campaign created the ad and
he defends it.
Since Tuesday, there's been national bipartisan backlash to the ad.
For NPR News, I'm George Shilcock.
The Kremlin says it is willing in principle to resume peace talks involving Ukraine and
American mediators.
But Ukrainians are incensed with the Trump administration's praise of a Russian government
that launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine in 2022.
NPR's Joanka Kisses reports on development since the White House's key envoy met with
the heads of Ukraine and later Russia.
After Steve Woodkopf arrived in St. Petersburg, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced
Russia was freeing American teacher Stephen Hubbard from captivity.
Woodkopf responded by calling Putin a humanitarian.
That angered Aleksandr Maresko, who leads the Ukrainian Parliament's Foreign Affairs
Committee.
It's a total disgrace for America, for American diplomacy and even for President Trump.
It's like calling Hitler humanitarian in the middle of the Second World War.
Putin is committing genocide against Ukrainians.
Ukrainians see Putin as the driving force behind the longest and deadliest war in Europe since
World War II.
Joanna Kisses, NPR News, Cave.
Well, a survey of homebuilders in the U.S. shows the industry has not been this pessimistic
about the housing market in at least a decade.
More from NPR's Stephen Bizaha.
The National Association of Home Builders Survey for October found there has not been
this much pessimism since 2012, when the housing market was still recovering from the Great
Recession.
The association also reports that the price of goods used for homebuilding, including energy,
was up almost 10 percent in September, year over year.
All this gloom is also showing up in new home permits in September.
They were down about 3 percent from a year ago.
There's just not much demand for buying homes right now with high mortgage rates.
The National Association of Realtors reports that pending home sales in September were
down more than 11 percent from a year earlier.
That's Stephen Bizaha reporting.
This is NPR News.
Hundreds of people in Toledo, Ohio are being forced to evacuate their homes or shelter
in place because of the risk of a toxic release.
A chemical tank exploded last night.
Former President George W. Bush's brother says on Facebook that he voted early in the
midterms and it was for Democrat James Talarico in Texas.
Neil Bush said in yesterday's post that Republican Ken Paxton's role in a legal challenge of
the 2020 elections outcome was an affront to Democratic institutions.
Bush, who describes himself as a longtime Republican, says he has never met Talarico
but sees integrity and humility in the Democratic Senate nominee.
Oysters are critical to the health of the Chesapeake Bay, located in the mid-Atlantic
between Maryland and Virginia, over harvesting his decimate of their ranks, but Ari Daniel
reports one man is working to bring them back.
John Consoli of Eastern Maryland marvels at these mollusks.
I think I'm more enthusiastic about something that's like a rock than anybody else could
possibly be.
He started by growing them off his pier.
Oh, this one's heavy, hold on, this is what I need my son, hold on.
But ever since he got hooked, he can't help but spread the good word within his community
that includes neighbors, his dental hygienist, and a local restaurant.
It teaches me just how something that seems so insignificant can make a difference.
Consoli estimates his networks helped add well over a million oysters back to the Bay.
For NPR News, I'm Ari Daniel.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.
